The longer the matter is delayed the more diflit-ult it will become : and in the opinion of the writer it is high timo public opinion was aroused. It was mid when the purchase of the Gas Works was contemplated, that too high a price was being asked—that if bought the Corpora- tion would be heavily burdened and possibly the ratepayers he called upon to provide out I of the ordinary rates of the town for the payment of some portion of the annuities and interest due to the proprietors. No doubt the people who said these things fully believed them. and they acted up to their belief by carrying the question to a poll. What however has been the result ? Managed by a committee of the Corpora- u ride, is not supposed to bestow that particular attention and care that ordinary proprie- tors bestow upon their business, they have proved I that the faith was well-founded whMh the pro- motors of the purchase had in the growth and expansion of the town, and consequently in the increase of the demand for gas. Looking over the I accounts of the Corporation, so far as they can be I understood, the Committee appear to have reduced , the price of gas to the consumer nd. per thousand I feet, and to knee saved no less a sum than £15,000, besides repaying annually one-fiftieth part of the cost. Sot only have they reached this happy condition, but every year that comes the profits must increase ; for, the Sinking Fund being reduced, the interest must reduce al., and the ratepayers may in the not dietant future expect a substantial assistance to the rates from this much contested purchase. Taking these circumstances into consideration, and arguing from the same premises, it seems not unreasonable to expect that,if the Corporation were to purchase the Waterworks undertaking, similar results would follow. BT. PETER'S ANNUAL TEA PARTY. The annual tea party in connection with St. Peter's Church, Warrington, was held in the achool- room, John-st., on Monday evening. The under- mentioned ladies presided at the tea table. :---Mrs. Willis. Mrs. Willcocks, Mrs. Gibson Smith, 3lrs. Brown, Mrs. Blease, Mrs. RiCIIRTd9OI2, Mrs. (ire., , Miss White, Mies Harvey, the Nlisses Cawley. the I' Misses Balshaw, and the Al if+SeS Edgar. At the , subsequent entertainment the Vicar. the Rev. T. Rigby, occupied the chair, and was supporned by the, 7 Rector of Warrington (Rev. F. W. Willis), Mr. Robert Davies, and the Rev. W. L. Warne. In opening the proceedings, the Cliairmm said the fact that they had now to use that schoolroom for all purposes was vet y disagreeable, and he was sure . the parishioners would be no less happy than he when they saw the foundation-stone of a new r church laid. (Applause.) One of the great difficul- ties in the way hitherto had been the want of a cite, but Mr. William Sham had now generously given • one. (Applause.) Towards the building fund they had a little money, but of course they ' wanted more. (Laughter.) The Building Com- mittee hoped to begin operations before very , long, and it would be generally admitted that the church was greatly needed. (Applause.)— , Mr. Hobert Davieo remarked that if anyone bad any- thing to say against Warrington he was up in arose directle, he was for the' defendant" at once. (Laughter and ajtplause.) lie felt quite sure, and he could tell from what lie had seen, there had been a marlool improvement in many ways in the town of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Ile was old enough to remember it when it had only 18,000 of a population, and seeing party after patty go ilowu Bridge-st. to fight pitched battles in Arpley Netts every Saturday afternoon. There were at that time only two constablee—Paul Caldwell, and a deputy named Jones. (Laughter.) In addition there IVOIT the parish constables, an honorary officer, one of whom Ives pretty n(gularly his (Mr. Davi.'s) father, who at the saine time served the office of rector's warden ,at the parish chord,. Ile land seen men stripped to their waists tight for threeoptarters of an hour on a Sundae morning at Market Gate. But despite such occurences then) was never any serious crime in Warrington. (Hear, (tear.) In that parish they wanted a church and a parsonage, and they needed help in order to obtain them. There were many calls upon onto pursue in Warrington, but one of the most urgent at the present time (ammo, to he that of building a church for the parish of St. Peter. flu should therefore put down Ids name for £5O in order to assist that object. (Applanset—The Rector I remarked that the Building Committee held a meeting on Friday at which it was agreed that the great want of the parish—a church—should be supplied as *Mtn as possible. (Applause.) It was felt that the ;ample needed a church and that the church should be mode as worthy of God as they could ; yet that they ought to act in the most practical and sensible manner, and not spend (heir money on too broad a scheme, too large an undertaking. (Hear, hear.) They decided that they would have a chaneel, and a nave, and vestries ; that if they could do more they would. (Appfituse.) He asked a very liberal gentleman, WIIO had built a ((lurch how much it cost. s' (sell, he said, " I did riot (get much cliangej out of £15,000." That Ming so, he consideml that they ought to be prepares to spend one-thied of that sum—£s,ooo. (Hear, hear ) Sotne pemple had a very erroneous notion of the value of livings. Fle saw a statement itt a newspaper the other day that the living of Warrington was put down at £2,00(i a year. In reply to that very erroneous state- ment lin might say that he should very sows compiete hi': first year at Warrington, and so (ache had received £2OO only, and the cost of coming in had been nearly £l,OOO. Out that when such figures were given his hearers needed to remember that they were very often greatly over-stated, and that there were very litany outgoings, so that what was put down as a very large stun in the gross was ((Ben reduced to £3OO or so a year. div.head: SUICIDE OF PIGOTT.
div.p: THE SUICIDE OF PIGOTT.

It has been placed absolutely beyond doubt that the man who committed suicide in the Hotel Embajadnres, Madrid, was Richard Pigott. Pigott arrived at Madrid feint Paris on Thursday forenoon, and wee secured at the railway station by an interpreter tout in the service of the Hotel Esubatadorea and by him taken to that lintel. He carried only a small handle.. but he was very well dressed, and to the hotel nivel., seemed a well-to-do treveder of the ordinary British tourist type. His ap- pearance, in fart. warranted the hotel clerk assigning him one of Ate hest rooms in the house, and Pigott made hininelf an learn as though he had always been usol to the best acrommedintion. Ile arranged with the interpreter to attend upon him , dining his stay, as he explained he did not speak Spanish, and he knew little French. After taking re- i frisitnvnta. Pigntt said he wanted to telegraph to , tendon, and at his request the interpreter showed hien • the way to the telegraph office. There in the inter- priaer's prenmen he wrote out a telegram which the police have sine. ascertained IVIAR addrenned to "Shea. non. Mi. Inn Fields, London,- and asked for something prireini Inn he sent to him. After despatch- ing this telegram Pigott seemed quite happy, and with the interpreter visited the museum, the cathedral church of San Isidro and other rights of the city, and strolled round the Puerto del Sol. He dined well at the hotel in the evenine, and retired to bed at an early hour, after making inquiries whether a teleerate had arrived for him. Alronst the first thing Pigott did when he went down in the meriting won to sok whether the expected telegram had arrived, and he vented wor- ried at again receiving a reply in the negative. He moved about in an :Li mires. restlesa kind if risc. and his evident anxiety at length began to attract ialention, which is a had thing for a atoms,. in Spain. The hetet people gave information to the pollee reverting their restless Rue,t, red the police received a telegram from London Ovine Pirett'il description and slating that he was in Madrid. Fly four o'clock nn Friday after- noon the detectives had ran their fox to earth. At ball- past trey police officers arrived at the hotel, and after queetionine the interpreter satisfied themselves that Pleott was the man they wanted. Mr. Roland Parisonby, alias Pigott, was in his bedroom on the trot floor, and the scared interpreter and the police officer in 'hart. proceeded. The interpreter topped at the floor, and vas 'old to come in. Tie entered the room and told Pigott hat a police immecter wanted to speak to him. Pigott turned deathly pale, and for a °lenient seemed In loose his nerve completely. But he von pulled him- self together, and ealinla told the interpreter that " It wax all right Ile would are the gentleman." At this moment the inspect, entered the room, and Pigott, inutferine witnethilie al sii e his limeade. ...peed back a Pare or tarn and tmened the linndhag, which lay upon a cheir. The inspector then areing•l to divine Pigott's object, and serene forward to seize him. It was too late. Pientt had a hig revolver in his hand, pietist] the muzzle against his mouth, drew the trigger, and fell to the ground a horribly mutilated corpse. Soon after- warrla the chief of police, to whom iniormation of the nnicidethad been sent he special mesteneera arrived at the hotel. and in the presence of the oval judicial offi- cials F4/1/8 were 'twee] upon the dead n.n'a Thew wens few in newton. and nf little value, In ilre bag were found two or three shirts and some socks. all quire new. There were in the poeketn of the clothes which he wan wearing whim he committed suicide, and which, in fact, were all Is. enuentsett in the war of wear- ing apparel, a number of note-books, cheque-bet., and received letters, red other odds and ends were found in the various pockets. In the pocket of the overcoat was found an official-looking document, which on investieit- tion proved to be a police license, dated Dublin. and authorisine Richard Pigott, journalist, to carry a revoli yen. A letter war found in the hand-bag. addressed In Mr. Henry •Labouehere, M.P. The envelope was clonely sealed. and ready to be put Into the post. This epistle. probably the Hat written by the forgerbi hand. rem.. • in substance the confession of guilt fillkfie by Pigott lo • Mr. Labonehere in the presence of Mr. Kiht. Pigott often referred to bin •meetinea and ronvervitions with Mr. Labouchere. lie says say that the first bateh of letters which I sold to The Times Were genuine. The screed lot, however, contained several forged letters. Among the letters in this batch which I forged were two attributed to Mr. Parnell. one purporting to be written by Michael Devitt, one bar Mr. Jas. F. (Melly, at.P.,and one by Mr. Patrick Egan." After furtive reference to the for- geries Pigott wrote I do asatire you 'lint I in, deeply vrry for all the wrong than I have roomed Mr. Parnell sad others. and I am ready to place in your hands the means of repairing that wrong. and 1,10 all in my maser to mend matters. All that I have hitherto said is false. hut what I have written under oath is true." A second letter signed by Finale. and else addressed to Labourhere. was found in the pocket of the undenmat. It is dated Monday last, anti wan evidently written in London, pro- hahly with the intention of poetine it on the journey. To Warringt,s, Wit,w.,rks --are they ever to lent roe the property id the born That is a question which is often put; but we seem to he a log way as yet frmn obtaining a definite answer. There ism be no doubt as to is general feeling amongst ratepayers that the undertaking ought to, belong to the town ; but the question of seeking to effect a purchase is allowed to drift, and drift, in the belief that the Waterworks Company will Ind be satisfied with anything Ws than an exoti- taut price. Mt.ennvnile tliu price, whatever it may b., is inermising year by year, which means that the longer the (.lirporation delay the purchase the mere in the end they will have to pay. Mr. JOHN Cerwri mid, when he was Mayor, approached the Company with a view to laying their terms before the Two Council, but the figures named were, we believe, so high that he declined to take the responsibility 14 even presenting them to the Cor- p, orati• m. l'ed a le% must be made some- time, and SOI/1.'1,,w, and to this end it has seemed to us desirable to place the matter before our rendez, or that th,y may at any rate give expres- sion to their views 011 the subject. It not ;infre- quently Imppens, when there is a bargain to be struck, that those who ultimately heroine parties to it are a long Way tilt each other, to commence with. They approach each other by degrees, until, by what ADAM Sarni calls the higgling of the market, a figure is agreed upon which is fair to both parties to the transaction. It will lie seen that the kill is set rolling this week by " Citizen" who, in another column, contributes a thought- lid and carefully prepared article on the subject. "Citizen" is a townsman of posi- Con who has at heart the interests of the

town. but he does not make his name public, as lie thinks the subjeet will be emre likely to be discisad impartially if it is discussed imperson- ally. It will be noted that he has a strong opinion 144 to the desirability of a water monoply being in the possession of the Corporation, and as to this we are in perfect agreement with him ; but when he CI tines to deal with the question of revenue and of purchase we are inclined to think that he takes too r.y a view of the matter. He suggests that if the Waterworks became the property of the Cor- poration, working expenses might he cut down ; and so they might, but except as to the saving of directors' fees, we are afraid it would be found that working expenses would increase rather than '• Citizen is hold enough to take the bull by the horns in considering the question of purchase from the point of view of the highest sum likely to be asked by the shareholders of the Com- pany ; and, as he states the case, the figures do not look very formidable. But the Company are , net as yet obtaining " the full interest or dividend to which by lawthey are entitled," and we submit that it would be inequitable for the Corporation to effect a purchase upon that basis. The shareholders are certainly entitled to something beyond current dividends, if it Call be shown that dividends are undoubtedly on the increase ; and that something should be a figure somewhere between what they think they (night to have and what, in the first instance, the Corporation would be inclined to offer. But we are anticipating in some measure the criticism of our readers, to whom our columns are open for the discussion of this important ques:ion.

Tns suicide of Proorr —shocking as suicide always is—cannot be said to be unnatural. It was suggested from the moment of his disappear- ance that be might destroy himself. Ho was not the kind of man, however, to resort to self- slaughter from any feeling of remorse ho had been too long inured to villainy to do that ; and if he could have found a wealthy newspaper pro- prietor to supply him with another thousand pounds or so, he would have sought to get further • out if the way and to prolong his wretched exist- ence. lint penniless, a Police Inspector at his heels, and the prospectbefore him of imprisonment for life, it is not surprising that he should make deadly use of a revolver. What does not cease to suprise all who reflect on the miserable career of this miserable forger is that the " Tines " should have staked its money and its character upon a man who was without character at all. Granted that thieves sometimes betray thieves, it is not I usual to reward the informer until it is proved that his inb•rmation is reliable. The '• Times ' in , the fullness—or perhaps we should say in the bitterness -of its heart, paid away its thousands without asking for anything from Pim= in the nature of proof. It has shown itself blind as never bat was Mind ; and, as it has insisted, without justilicatiomin murdering reputations,there can be no sympathy with it when the time comes for it to undergo its ptinishunint. It is just possible that the Parnellitm, in the jubilation of feeling arising out of the exposure of the foul ! 14,4 to ruin them as a Party, may be more or leas indifferent as to taking action , against the " Times -; lust it is a quest' of justiee and not of private feeling, and justice demands, in the public interest, that he who is gmlty of a great wrong shall have commensurate punishment meted out to him. The ships of the Reserve and Training Squadrons have been ordered to repair to their respective ports for overhaul and refit during the first week of next month, exactly . at the time when the Channel Squadnm is due to Nturn from the Mediterranean.

The Earl of Milton has given notice that on an early day he will present a hill rendering liable to corporal 1111 l ishment " persons cimvicted of burg- ! lary, or attempted burglary, and found in the prissiiiision of firearms' The lash has been found ii genuine deterrent to garrotters, and it tnight have a wholesome effect on tire-armed burglars. • It is certainly worth trjing.

King Milan, of Se—rvia, has abdicated in favour of his thirteen-year old son. He has not been snows, either as a ruler or as a soldier, while the diffhrences with Queen Nathalie are notorious. It is stated that of late, he has suffered from a ner- vous malady which has impaired Ins reason. He has, therefore, good reason for laying aside the crown : and it is to be hoped that his head may he a little easier.

The Welsh residents of Earlestown and district are to be congratulated on the success of their Eisteddfod, which was held at Earlestown on Satur- day. Mr. high, M.P.,who presided. " tumbled to" the affilir no readily that Mr. W. Rawlins, in proposing a vote of thanks, jocularly alluded to " the view of national feeling he had displayed." ; Perhaps when Mr. Legh has had a little more training he will be prepared to vote for Home ! Rule for Wales. We are travelling in that direction, and Mr. Legh is something of a traveller.

It was a matter of course of ter the committees had had their treat of pudding that the manager shosld have his treat of praise. Ile W 149 only having what he had paid for. lint what was the meaning of the reference to the first class hall, and the second class hail? Are thesheop divided from the goats, and which lis which ? It sounds like a hit f old fashioned !Toryism, the very essence of which is" class "

Certain of the Tories and Liberal Unionists are aiready beginning to hedge on the Home Role question. They perceive that HOMO Rule must come, and they have beg to talk about a confer- ence of all parties. They want to save their seats by a show of conciliation, though they had nothing to say when Mr. Gladstone urged the Tories to ; take the matter up on their coming into office. ' Let these men deliver themselves to Lord Salis- bury ; he is their leader And he has a majority behind him. The public have had enough of Round Table Conferences.

There is some danger of a split in the Women's Suffrage movement. Mr. Woodaffs hill seeks to confer the Parliamentary franchise upon uninarried females who pay rates and taxes—as is the case with the municipal franchise. But there is a sec- tion who, standing their ground logically, demand that the franchise shall he conferred on married as well as single women. Hence the risk of a split. There is sin chance, however, in the present Par- liament of going beyond Mr. Woodall's bill, and those who cminot get the whole loaf insist he con- tent, for a time, with half a loaf.

Councillor Voisey did good work, at the meet- ing of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday, in getting a motion passed for a statement to be prepared showing what are the available profits from the Gas Works. There is something to the good ; that everybody knows ; but it is not clear whether there is a sum large enough to permit of a reduction in the price of gas, or a reduction of the ' rates. There is nothing to he gained by flounder- ing in the deck; and it is to be hoped the Garr Committee will appreciate Mr. Voisey's action I when his cry, like Goalie's, is—" More light, more light." Mr. Gent-Davies who was spoken of by Mr. T. P. O'Connor as having been" convicted of fraud," has resigned an member for the Kennington Divi- ion of Lambeth by accepting the Chiltern Hun- dreds. As thin is an office under the Crown we have the anomaly of a Tory Government appoint- ing a Tory official who has been "convicted of fraud." Mr. Gent-Davies ought really to have been , expelled from the House: and Mr. W. H. Smith had his attention called to the matter on Tees- day evening. Mr. Smith shirked his responsibil- ity . • he is leader of the House, but then he does not lead.

The question of steaming in weavinesheds Jvcoming a question of practical politics. A ' special inquiry in Blackburn, made some months ago, resulted in au expression of opinion that, as practiced, it was highly injurious to health. The ' use of steam is good for weaving, but it is not good for the weaver. Fancy turning out of a weaving shed with clothing saturated with mo;sture during such weather as we have had this week! Nothing could be better for the cultivation of rheumatism and bronchitis. Parliament is to be asked to act in the matter, and it is to be hoped it will act speedily.

LANCASIIIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION. THE REV. .1. YONDE ELECTED PRESIDENT.

IThe annual business ,neeting of the Lancashire Congregational Union was held at the Grosvenor-nt. Chapel, Manchester, on Thursday. Mr. W. Shaw, ' Oldham, the genend treasurer, presided. A resolu- tion in favour of Sunday closing of ',Odic houses was adopted without discussion. The Rev. .t. Yonge, Warrington. having received the highest vote in toe ballot for the election of President dlf the was elected to that office for the ensuing year. An alphabetieal list of tire ehurclies air-ding assistance from the union fends wili gone throtigh, and grants to the amount of .C 2.152 Is. /GI. were made.—The Rev. A. Poster conlially invite.l the untorr to meet at Blackburn next year. The invitation was , accepted.. -Mr. W. Shaw was unanimously re-elected treasurer of the onion, and thanks were tendered to the general secretaries for their services during the past year. They were afterwards n.-elected. , The new President of the Lancashin, Congrega- tinned Union, the 111's. Yonge, has been pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, for several years. He was born in tire year ISAS, in the Strand, London, nearly opposite Ese'er Hall. Ile is the nephew of tlke late Rev. W. C. Yonge, Il4rmerly ,of Brentford, and also of Mr. George Yonge, who for many years was secretary to the British Society for the Propagation of the Gospel among the Jews. Mr. Yonge was educated for the ministry at Cheshunt College, and in 18112 he settled at East Cowen, Is/e-of-Wight. Ito remained there for forte years, until 181fft, when he resigned his charge, and accepted a call to Heywood, Manchester, where lie WilS pastor for ten years. During his ministry in that town anew church and , school were built, at a cost of .tiB,lloll, and aloo a branch school. NH. Yonge succeeded the Rev. 0. S. Heaney in tire pastorate of Wycliffe Church, Wlll.- rington. Ile has for several years been secretary of the Lancashire Congregational Unioti for the Liverpool district, and last year was President of the Manchester Congregational Board.

ALLEGED PERJURY AT WARRINGTON. At the Borough Police Court, yesterday morning. Thomas Mannion, a labourer, was brought up in custody on a charge of having committed perjury while giving evidence at the County Petty SI•88i0119, on the '..1./th ult., in a case in which Frederick Simpson was the informant, and David Bmmhall the defendant. Mr. Jenkins, who appeared for the prosecution, mid that be was instructed by the Cheshire Lines Committee. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on the date named in the charge, David Bramhall, of 30, Ilaydock-st., was charged on the information of Frederick Simpson. chid of police on the Cheshire Lines rail- way. with having. on the 25th of January, travelled from Warrington to Glasebrook with- out having paid his fare, with intent to avoid payment. Bramhall was lined for the offence. The prisoner in the preaent case was railed by the then defendant Bramliall, and, after having been duly sworn, he stated tut he mw Bramhall at the Warrington Central Station on the morning of the day on which Bramhall was alleged to have travelled without n ticket. Gestated that he saw Bramliall purchase a ticket, and that he travelled with him as far as Padgate. In cross-examination prisoner stated that the train in which he and Bramhall travelled left the Central at about eight o'clock in the morning. That was the time at which the defendant Bramhall travelled, but it would be proved that it was impossible for prisoner to have gone to Padgate by the some train as he swore he had done, because the train did not stop at Padget°. The Company, having regard to the different ways in which they were robbed by unscrupulous permna, felt it their duty to prose- cute Mannion.—J. R. Buckton, clerk to the County Magistrates, gave formal evidence as to the hearing of the charge against Bramhall, and produced the information on which the said charge was founded. On the hearing of that charge prisoner Mannion gave evidence on behalf of the defendant, and the oath was administered to him by witness: Frederick Simpson, Oarston, chief of police on the Cheshire Lines railway, said that on the 20th ult. David Bramhall was charged with the offence named by the last witness. The prisoner gave evi- dence on Bmmhall's behalf, and said "I saw Beam. halt at the Warrington station. I new him take a : ticket and pay for it, and I took a ticket to Padgate at the same time, and I travelled with him in the same compartment to Padgate. It was about eight : o'clock in the morning. It was four weeks ago on Friday." Witness took rough notes of the evidence given by the primner.—Joseph Wilson Davies. assistant booking clerk at the Central station, , produced the train book, which showed what : tickets were issued to filaoubrook on the 25th of , January. The books also allowed what tickets ' were issued to Padgate that day. There were no third class tickets tamed to 01v...brook by the 8.7 a.m. train. Three were issued by the 9.6 a.m., the numbers being 5.894 5,593, and 5.894. Three more , were issued by the 10.34 a.m., being numbered 5,895- 6-7. By the 2.15 p.m. train numbers 5,895-9 were issued. By the 5.30 train one ticket only. numbered I 5,900 was imited. No other tickets for Glazebrook I were lousiest on that day. Witness was premnt in Court when the can. against Bramball was heard. div.head: EXTRAORDINARY CAREER OF A YOUNG coerLE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CAREER OF A YOUNG coerLE.

I Edward Kemp and Louisa O'Brien. a young couple lof respectable appearance, were brought before Major Halm:horst and Mr. 0. L. Wigg, at Runcorn Police Court yesterday, charged with having on the 2nd November last feloniously stolen an overcoat, a pair of trousers, a silk handerchief and a pair of socks, the property of John Brannon, labourer. From the statement of Mr. J. O. SwifL'of St. Helens, who defended, it appeared that Kent was IS years of age, and was the son of a pork butcher, who carries on business in one of the chief thoroughfares in Birmingham. The girl was 17 years of age and had earned a livelihood as a tailoress. Mr. Swift produeed a bundle of temtimonies which showml that the girl had borne a good character,andhad taught in the Sun- day schma. The couphibivameacquaintedat church, and Kemp's parents anti friends, objected to the intimacy. In NIA-ember the prisonms eame to Liverpool with the girl's mother, who became separated from them, and they werefieft lathe city without any means of livelihood or any chance of obtaining employment. They went into three lodginghouses, and committed three separate rob'' furies, and then cause to Runcorn, where they stopped a night so nianand wife at Mrs. Stanton's lodgingliousein I Granville-st. The theft of which they were now accused was then committed ami the prisoners after- wards went on to St. Helens, and committed a further robbery. With the proceeds of these robberies the pri- mmer: returned to Birmingham, but instead of going to their friends they took up Usti!' alesie in a lodginghouse, and having started on a career of crhne, apparently could not stop themselves, for they again committed a robbery. They were apprehended by the Birmingham police, to wit, enthey tnade a full confession and with the whole facts before them, the magistratim sentenced them to two months imprisonment. Afterwards they were sentenced to a month's further imprisonment by the Livens-sit inagistrates, followed by a fortnight's impri- sonment for the offences committedat St. Helens. They were apprehended by Sergeant thmling on their release, , and were now brought before their Worships to vim- plete the chapter. Mrs. Kemp was present to take charge of her on, and the female prisoner's former I employer I,osl promised to take her track. Mr. Swift suggested that the iirisoners had Imes punished suffich ently, and the Bench, being of the same opinion, passed , the 110111inni sentence .of one days imprisonment.—Mrs. Kelllp, with much heeling. thanked their Wonthirm for I their clemency. Mr. Swift stated that she had spent a : large amount of money in compensating the personswho I had lost their pr, opery through the prisoners.

• . society wo i uld never have been n as present proud posi- tion, being regarded by all the leading men of the day as a true example of what might In done by combination and industry. (Applause.) It was also a true symbol that they might by th,,ir perwital industry and perseverence raiSe themselves and fatal,vi to such comfortable positions that when they were about casting off the cares of this life, they might be able to lie down to rest with the soothing thoughts . that they had done their duty both to their familini and to their friends, and had not wasted the tali•nts their , Maker had been (Am.,! to bestow upon thin, but had ! used them with advantage to themselves and credit to those with whom they had beennsinected. (Applause.) I On the other side of the shield they found the cross keys ! and the lamb, emblions of security and pen.. The I golden keys taught them a silent lesson that, although their doors were xi firmly secured, they were always ready to lie opened to those who were in distress, and ! Will) had believed in their institution, and by the means hell forth inade provision for their future. They were slain type that nth° keys of the Church denotisl power and authority to preach the el,.pel and adininister the Sacraments and to exercise government and discipline, that men might be achnitted to or exclude,' from the Church as was roper;', so their keys denoted the inwer and authority their officers had to administer government and discipline in their ranks. The lame wet% a true type of humility and peace towanis all men, denoting to them that they ought stall times to be willing to sacri- fice their own pleasure and trouble to assist those who required it more than themselves, and endeavour to show to the world that their object as a swiety west° live In pegri, and happlF)o.l with all their fellow men. Yet these contrasted types of life pP:sent and life to come, of mans &ay and man's destiny, were separated and vet united by a golden esma, bearing the triple flower of their nation, the row, thistle and shamnwk, and recently the leek of Wales. It al., told them that in the forma- tion of their order they had not despises' tlx, people of theirsister countries, but had united thein.,lves together in one common bond of loste—Englislinien, Irishmen, , Scotehmen, and Welshmen, to spread wide the noble . principles and precepts of their brotherhood, by render- ing those good services for which they had been called , together, awl holding forth that right hand of fellowshijs ' that Was so well known in their lodges. (Applause.) ! Commenting on the words of one of the noblest mottoes tithe Order—friendship, love, and truth—he said tlmt in their endinVours to bold forth the advantagea of their Order, they had not forgotten their old and esteemed , masters, but had respected their memory by inscribing the mottoes in one of the first and most beautiful of languages. (Applause.) They had also inscribed it in Latin to show that they would TiOt discard the past, but would learn from it. They had, he believed, adopted it in that form because it was not a changeable language, and by no doing would go down from one generation to another unithangnl. (Applause.) Allusion was nude to the globe, which, he said, reminded them that in pro- moting the welfare of their Order, their ramifications had extended all over the universe ;" indeed, the whole of the emblem was a silent sermon, gathering up gible signs, Jewsia of eager energy, of lofty aspirations. I of world wide sympathy and of honest endeavours, all ! conseeratal be sacritiee ; but :ebove all, belonging as it I were to a higher region, from winch there looks down I the great and universal eye. (Applause.)—P. P. G. M. Miller, in proposing a vote of thanks to the lecturer, said it had been to them a truly interesting and instructive lesson, which, if taken to heart, would encourage Owen, to forward the noble cause.— P.D. LOCAL CASES AT THE QUARTER SESSIONS.
The Liverpool County Ses4ons were opened at the Sessions House, Liverpool, on Tuesday. and con- chided on Wednesday. The following local cases were heanl.—

Tire PIANO SWAM. AT WARRINGTON. On Tuesday Jam. barley (45), ironmoulder, pleaded not guilty to fraudulently takingand converting to his own Utie a piano of which he was the bailee. Mr. Cottingham prosecuted. The prisoner signed a hiring agreement with Aaron Price, who traded as the British Furnishing Company, 10, John-nt., Warrington, and bought the piano for 36 guineas, on the usual hiring terms. He only paid £2 and afterwards parted with the piano to another furniture broker, after which he went off to Glasgow, when he was arrested. The pri- soner mid it was his wife who sold the piano, but evidence was given that he himself called on the broker bra portion of the money, £6 Wing given to him, and that in his presence his wife said the piano was absolute- ly their own. They kept a provision shop, and had received the piano front a custmner in settlement of a large account. Whenarrestsl the prisoner said he never stole the piano, nor did lel rive his consent to the iintrument being taken from his house ; it was all his wife's fault, and he had received no money. lh gave the police officer £l4 before he a ryes ttd . Theprisoner said he did not know the terms of the hiring agreement, the business being transacted by his wife. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentence was deferred. On Wed- nesday Martha Varies., 40 yeats of age, described as a shopkeeper, the wife.of the prisoner in the pnivious case was found guilty of having fraudulently converted to her own use a hired piano. In this case also the piano was obtained on the purchase-hire system and shortly after- wards disposed of to broke.. Martha barley was sent to jail for six weeks and her husband for four weeks. Upon the arnst of Jones Variety in Glasgow he gave up to the police £l4, and this amount the c tart ordered to , be distrilmted between the broken vietimised, each in proportion to his loss. The broken were ordered to give up the pianofortes to the rightful owners without any payment in respect ti the money advanced by them , to theprisoners. ACTS.. ATTACK ON A ilAir.Errllir AT IirIITOICWOOD. George Sephton and James Rawson were indicted for having. at Buttonwood, on the night of the fith Feb., been tound on certain land in the occupation of Thomas Perks anneal or the pursuitargante,and also for wound- ing George Robert Lee, a gamekeeper in the employ of the Hon. lampold W. H. Powys. The counsel for the pnseetition was Mr. Foard, Mr. Collingwooet Hope defending—The case of the prusectition having closed. Mr. Hope raised a technical objection, contending that I had not been proved, in accordance with the require- ments of 9 Geo. IV., chap. 69, in elven occupation the land was, though it was quite true that this information was net forth in the indietment.—After some eGliversil- Oen between the counsel and the bench, the gamekeeper was recalltar by the inatriatrates, and he testified that the land was in the occupation of the His. Leopold Powys, the owner.—Tlmugh this was in contradiction of the tenns of the indictment, Mr. Hope contended that the charge fell to the ground, and that the prisoners must be discharged. It was further pointed out by the defending counsel that, though die prisoners werecharged with wounding, it had been clearly dawn by the evidence Oat a bruise only had Lott intlictsl, and that no skin had been broken. (Lee appeared in court with his arm in a sling.) The magistrates held that theobjec- don Was good, and, at their threetion, the jury found the prisoners not guilty, and they were arotrdingly dis- charged. Hr. Hope said that, had his objection been unavailing,he had a perfectly good defence on the inerits of the caw, and would have called witnesses to prove au alibi.

-- HIGHWAY BOARD WORK. Sir,-1 wish to bring a matter beton. the Vrarrington District Highway Board, viz., all the mile stones from Warrington o Hollins Green are placed too far back in the hedges, and the said distances are all obliterated. I have expected Mr. Thompson to have had them re-let- tered a long time ago ; but I fear he has overlooked the matter. It looks more like civilisation when finger posts and mile stones are legible, and footpads can know where they are going and how far they have travelled.— Yours he., FOOTPAD.

THE RUNCORN SHIP CANAL MISSION. Sir,—ln your report of the opening id the new Mimion Hall last week you said that "the Mariner's Church was vented" ho. Will you please correct this statement* for the church was lent to us free for as long a time as we wanted it, and therefore no nmney Ims been paid for the use of it. A year ago when I came to Runcorn the Rev. Mr. Preston offered us the little church, although he knew nothing about the missionary, nor yet the kinsl of services he would conduct in it. We are all very thankful to him kw his kindness.—Yliurs fait JOHN WXISON, Missionary.

THE WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL. This is the first timo during the Society's existence that al-no dividend than £5 per cent. has been declaral, and if the shareholders will assist the directors in finding securities for their money, they may still rely on receiv- ing the larger dividend. The pr-vent directs retire tom office, and are oligible for mehrtion." The object of the society throughout had been to benefit the working- . classes as much as possible, by encouraging them in habits of frugality, and by enabling them to purchase property on easy and beneficial terms. NEW LOAN FROM SOUTH KENSINGTON.

The annual change bas just been made in the collection lent by the Science and Art Department to tile Warrington Museum. The new loan is of a more varied character, and rather more extensive. There are first, in the Art Gallery, the usual four , cases of specimens of industrial art, the branches I illustrated being glass, damask, bronzes, oriental I embroidery, carved and inlaid wood work, and I musical instruments, the latter chiefly of the lute and either type. Wood carving is also represented by six casts of old oak panels, lin frames on the wall, and in another room are about a score samples of oft lace, chiefly Belgian, French, and Italian. In addition, and as a new departure, there are six small oil paintings by Lucy, Clint, Ibbetson. netters, and Delfosse. The Science side of the Museum receives an Interest- ing addition to its Natural History olepart meta. A I case in which the disarticulated skeletons of a cat, is duck, and a codfish are arranged tide by side, is in , the Bird-room, and enlarged dissected models of a I silkworm anti a cluster of honey been on the comb I are in the case in the Fish "-room. In the same I case are also models, showing the structure of seven selected vegetable species. All the models are no large, it may be said so immense, as to exhibit the smallest parts clearly to the naked eye,the silkworm, for instance, being 27 inches long. Botanical students are further catered for by the exhibition of a series of large diagrams, with descriptions Will dried specimens representing fittof the natural orders of plants, which occupy the greater part of one side of the same room.

He mentioned this not as a perfert justification of the great poet's frailties, but as a palliation, and paid a very warm tribiate to the nobility of Burns' character and the sublime beauty of much of his poetry. But I think the following one of the best ruses ever , perpetrated. It was somewhere ii. the Forties that three noted wags, hard up for the wherewithal to pay for any more liquor, were on their way hot op one morning about one o'clock. They had disciosed various means of raising the wind when one of them, who, by the way, was minus one natural leg, hit upon a novel method, which was that he should take his wooden leg off and himself be put in a sack, his friends to carry him to the , "King's Head" under the pretence that he had been found drowned. It happened that at tide time there was a lady who presided at the above establishment, and she was mor- bidly afraid of inquests being held at her house, and the knowledge of this decided our bibulous crew to put their plan in operation, which they quickly did, though they had to knock herd to gain admatance, Once inside the portal of the "King's Head," however, they felt sure, as they dragged the sack in containing their one4gged friend.

Wodeven hear yo' gotten th' seek ?" "We've pood him eawt n' Feilden's lodge. an' ther'll hey to be a inquest—yo' nun led him lie here whol we fotch a constable; he'll nod hurt yn', poor chap.'. At thin the worthy hostess was almost paralysed wtth fear, but, being of a practical turn of mind, she at once appealed to them as a widow to take pity on her, offering them a gallon of beer and five shillings if they would take the uncanny burtben to some other hostel and say nothing about it. I needn't my that her good offer was at once closed with, hut the originator of the schema nearly upset their calculations, for when he heard how swimmingly his project was working, and how fast the beer was gurgling down the throats of his friends, he called out nearly loud enough for the lone widow to hear him, Heigh left' corpse sap!"

A DISAPPOINTED COUPLE.—On Saturday last a couple presented themselves at St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, as candidates for marriage, but owing to some misunderstanding there was no minister to perform the ceremony. The disap- pointed pair were therefore forced to return as they came, and remain single yet another day. They were, however, duly 'made one" on Sunday morning. SANKEY Bmtittooo WESLEYAN CHAPEL.- .0n Saturday evening, a unisical service, entitled "The railway train and its passengers," was rendered in the above chapel. The connective readings, descriptive of the sights and sounds witnessed an railways were given try Mr. It. En wistle. Recita- tions on similar subjects were rendered by Messrs. J. rotten and E. Wilkes, and dialogues by Misses A. !Dough and J. Woolley, and Messrs. T. Brough, J. Roderick, J. Wilkes, T. L George, H. Light, F. Light, and A. Fortes. Bright and appropriate choruses were given by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Brough. A collection was made in aid of the fund for building a new schoolroom. Cnossuiv-s, Misistox. -In aid of the funds of thin Mission, Whiell is in charge of the Rev. C. E. Jackson, a tea party and entertainment were held lin the Parochial Schools on Tuesday- evening. The 'principal portion of the programme at the entertain- ment was undertaken by Mr..l. H. Greenwood, of Manchester, who afforded great fun to the assembly. The following ladies and gentlemen also took part and contributed materially to the pleasure of the evening: —Mrs. Clayton, Mi.) Andrew, Miss Ethel White, Major Graham, and Mr. Snell. During the proceedings the Rector (MeV. F. W. Willis) and the Rev. C. E. Jackson delivered short addresses and thanked the crowded audience for their attendance and support. TRAP ACCIDENTS. —On Sunday afternoon, Mrs. Pugh and Miss Ilewitt, who reside at Newton-le- met with an accident at Warrington. They were driving a horse and trap, and when turn- ing into Winivick-st. from Crown-st., the horse stumbled and fell. The occupants of the vehicle ! were thrown out, but fortunately were not much hurt. They were attended by Dr. Cannel). On the evening of limo same day Mr. and Mrs. Jenkins. of Penketh, were driving along Buttermarket-st., when they met with a similar accident, being thrown out of their conveyance when near to the Inland Revenue Office. They were both badly shaken, and Mrs. Jenkins received injuries to the face and hands. She was taken to the Cross Keys, a public-house near by, and after resting there for a time, was con- veyed home in a cab. SUPPER AT THIS CONSERVATIVE CLUIL—Mr. Stanley Higham, the manager of the Conservative Club, on Monday evening entertained the members of the two Ball Committees and one or two friends to sapper. The gathering was held in the Com- , mittee-room. Councillor R. W. Francomb (chair- man of the club) presided, and Mr. John Roberts was in the vice-chair, and there were also present-- the Mayor, and Messrs. J. E. Wright, Alfred Woods, Henry Collin, George Woods, 11. J. Longton, G. F. F. W bite, T. Mason. B. Johnson, William Bloomfield, and Thomas Roberts. The healths of Mr. Ingham, Mr. Alfred Woods (secretary of the first class ball), Mr. 11. Collin (treasurer), Mr. John Roberts (chair- man ef the Committee of the second class ball), Mr. T. Mason (the treasurer), were drunk, and each gentleman suitably responded. STREET GAMBLING.—Tho other Sunday a man named Martin Lyons, who has appeared before the justices over a score of times, and two youths named Edward Flanagan and William Farrell, were amus- ing themselves by playing at pitch and toss in Cloth-hall yard when Constable Price, of the Borough force, made his appearance by way of the wall and caught them in the act. Summonses followed, and on Monday Lyons was fined 20s. and costs, Farrell 10s. and casts, and Flanagan he, and costs. At the same sitting of the Court, a youth named James Tobin was ordered to pay he, for , having played at pitch and toss in Erwood-st. last Sunday, while for having played cards for money M James-st., on the 23rd tilt, a man named Clifton I was fined ss. and costs, and four youths named I James Latimer. Arthur Latimer, Alphonse Cullen, and Edward Cartwright. were each fined ho. includ- ing costs. COURTSHIP AND MARRIAGE IN Six WEEKS.—A middle-aged couple named Molyneaux, whose grievances have been ventilated in the local Police !Court, have given point to the saying that to marry in haste means to repent at leisure. ESSAY ON JOHN MILTON.- —l3ll Saturday evening, at a meeting of the St. Paul's Mutual Im- hrrovcmenn Mr. I). Finney read a paper en- titled " John Milton." Mr. A. H. Jolley occupied the chair. The essayist commenced by taking a passing glance at the growth of the literature of England as leading up to the time of Milton. and proceeded to say that Milton was the list of the great Elixa- than writers, and, except Shakespeare, was by far the greatest and most illustrious. Milton was born in London in ItIOS, about 50 years before the great plagae. rec-iving his earlier education at St. Paints School. From there he went to Cambridge in 1025. His university career was brilliant anti distin- 'guished. It was probable that Milton conceivrtl the idea of Paradise Lost' from the Italian drama, but the unsettled state of affairs in England inter- rupted lam in his work forth) years. During the Cnnunonwealth he was engaged chiefly in writing political works in favour of the Cromwellian party. When Cromwell died he strove heart and Noel against the restoration, but could not prevent or even delay it. Through this, when the King re- turned, his life became in danger, but receiving t he Royal pardon, he settled in Bunhille-tields, London. It was in this quiet retreat that be finished aPara- dise Lost."
